images.after: What you give up when you refinance federal loans
images.title: What federal loans lose in a refinance
images.alt: Four cards on federal protections lost by refinancing privately: income-driven repayment, forgiveness, deferment and forbearance, and discharge.
images.caption: The switch can't be reversed. Once a federal loan becomes private, it stays private.

items.title: Income-driven repayment
items.text: Payments based on income and family size become a fixed schedule

items.title: Forgiveness programs
items.text: PSLF and other forgiveness apply only to federal loans

items.title: Deferment and forbearance
items.text: Private hardship policies are usually narrower

items.title: Discharge protections
items.text: Many private lenders don't offer the same; read the agreement

images.title: Refinancing federal loans: all must be true
images.alt: Checklist of four conditions for considering a federal loan refinance: stable income, no forgiveness plans, a comfortable standard payment, a lower rate.
images.caption: If you're unsure about any of these, keep the federal loans federal.

items: Stable income, with savings to cover a few rough months
No government or nonprofit job, and no forgiveness plans
A standard-plan payment you can comfortably make
A new rate low enough to matter over the life of the loan

images.after: So is now the right time?
images.title: Is now a good time for you?
images.alt: Comparison of situations where refinancing is worth a look, such as improved credit, against times it's usually a poor fit, such as a shaky job.
images.caption: The timing that matters is your own, not a guess about where rates are heading.

columns.label: Worth a look
points: Your credit score or income has improved
Your rate is well above today's offers

columns.label: Usually a poor time
points: Only a year or two of payments left
